Hybrid retrieval explained: Vector search, lexical search, and structured signals

How multi-lane retrieval systems combine complementary search modalities for robust recall

Hybrid retrieval combines dense vector embeddings, sparse lexical inverted indexes (BM25), and structured database filters to prevent single-strategy retrieval failures.

Short answer

Dense vectors capture meaning, lexical search captures exact terms, and structured queries enforce hard constraints; combining them creates a resilient retrieval pipeline.

Why single-modality retrieval fails#

Every individual retrieval paradigm has a well-documented failure mode. Relying on a single mechanism exposes an autonomous agent to systematic blind spots:

Retrieval ModalityPrimary IndexDistinct StrengthPrimary Failure Mode
Dense Vector SearchHNSW / IVF embeddingsSemantic paraphrasing and conceptual matchFails on rare tokens, numbers, and exact codes
Sparse Lexical SearchBM25 / Inverted indexExact keyword matching and rare identifiersFails on synonymy, polysemy, and vocabulary mismatch
Structured Assertion SearchB-tree / Relational SQLDeterministic boolean and numerical filtersFails on natural language inquiries with no schema match
Graph Path TraversalAdjacency index / Graph DBMulti-hop relational connections between entitiesFails on isolated facts lacking explicit edge extraction

How multi-lane search works in practice#

In a hybrid retrieval architecture, a user query is dispatched concurrently to multiple retrieval lanes against the same underlying corpus:

By evaluating candidates across multiple lanes, a document that scores moderately in vector search but matches an exact docket code in BM25 is elevated, preventing false negatives.

Fusion strategies: Score normalization vs rank fusion#

Once individual lanes produce candidate results, how should their scores be combined? Two strategies exist:

The hazard of score normalization

Dense vector cosine similarity produces scores in $[0, 1]$, while BM25 produces unbounded scores in $[0, \infty)$ depending on document length and term rarity. Combining raw or min-max scaled scores is brittle: one outlier score in BM25 can completely override vector relevance.

Rank-based fusion, specifically Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), solves this by ignoring raw scores entirely and evaluating the position of a document across lists: $RRF(d) = \sum rac{1}{k + r(d)}$. It requires no calibration and is mathematically stable.

The importance of pre-fusion scoping#

A critical design requirement in hybrid retrieval for agents is where authorization occurs:

  • Pre-filtering (Correct): Apply tenant, workspace, agent, and temporal filters before vector scanning or BM25 querying.
  • Post-filtering (Flawed): Retrieve top-k candidates globally and drop unauthorized results afterwards, leading to empty or truncated result sets.
  • Scope Preservation: Ensure fused results inherit the security bounds of the constituent lanes.

MESA's four-lane retrieval engine#

In MESA Core, the V4 retrieval router implements four distinct lanes: vector (via LanceDB), bm25 (via SQLite FTS5), assertion (via canonical SQLite tables), and graph (via Kùzu).

MESA applies dataset, tenant, agent, temporal, and jurisdiction constraints *before* lane execution. The public test fixture Alice knows Aurora verifies that when an assertion ranks #1 across all four lanes, its reciprocal rank fusion score computes deterministically to $4/61$. Read the execution details in How MESA Works.
